items.body: @Mark yes, but you could play Elite from tape.
There's a great writeup on Frontier Elite II here that might be an interesting read to you: jongware.com/galaxy1.html
@pjc50, 360 KB was the available space on a single-sided, double-density floppy disk.  No sensible developer of the time would load anything into memory that wasn't immediately required.

@user253751 - Well, it's likely most players would visit similar solar systems until they spread out over a sufficiently long distance (assuming the same spawning area). They won't need to consider thousands of solar systems before selecting one. The selection isn't permanent either (station relocation would be possible). The sheer massive size of the galaxy is also there to have in-between space. Distance will be a relevant factor for various things (time, fuel). But I would limit it to ~200-300m solar systems for the initial galaxy.

The player won't even consider 10000 worlds before selecting one. They'd have to spend Probably should have mentioned that it's multiplayer then: even if each player only looks at 1000 worlds, you might have 1000000 players who each want a different set of 1000 worlds, hence the requirement for so many worlds.

@user253751 - This is a challenge related to making the game good. In general, the game will have a variety of content, and exploration is just one aspect. Others are having star bases, defending/maintaining them, mining, producing, trading, research, and a major focus on combat (PvE and PvP). For that you may want to have a good strategic location. For that you need a sufficiently large world to select one. Guilds/factions may want to have their players' star bases in close proximity. Then you have to account for an unknown number of players, thus scalability.

What can the player actually do with these star systems? Can they travel to them? How fast can they travel? There is no way they will visit even ten thousand star systems before they get bored of playing.
@Mark much less than 360kb - it ran on systems which only had 48k available RAM.

@Battle I just meant that procedural generation is a good way to do this; that way you don't have to store anything (you just recompute it).  Also, that way you get to skip the boring database optimization and focus on making your game ;-)

@AC Well, for now I created a database with stars, planets, moons in a typical galaxy shape. I think the details about the optimization are not relevant. But out of curiosity (as I now plan to use Procedural Generation), what better way is there to store large amounts of data, if not a DB? As of "non-static" elements like missiles and ships, they are supposed to be saved in the server cache. Ships will be saved in intervals if they had any change to the DB, or on events like going offline.
